metaDescription: Five GE dehumidifiers from 25 to 50 pints compared by coverage, pump and Wi-Fi so you can match one to a bedroom, basement or large open floor.
expertTake: The GE 50-pint with the built-in pump is the pick for below-grade basements because it lifts water 15 feet. The 35-pint is the value pick for a mid-size room with a drain hose. Anyone drying a single closet or a small bathroom should skip GE's compressor line and buy a compact unit.
introParagraphs: A mainstream appliance maker's dehumidifiers lean on predictable controls, a front-access bucket and a drain port, and the real choice is the capacity step. Matching that step to the room avoids both an underpowered machine and an oversized one that cycles noisily.
Fan behavior, drain method and connectivity separate the models in a single range. Understanding how those features work helps you pay for the ones you will use and ignore the rest.

products.name: GE 50-Pint Dehumidifier with Pump and Hose, 5,000 Sq Ft
products.description:
This GE brings a lifting pump to a basement-sized machine. The pump pushes water up to 15 feet vertically through a hose, so you can drain to a laundry sink or outside without a floor drain nearby. Smart Dry, the brand's fan feature, adjusts airflow to the room humidity and drops noise once the room settles.

At 50 pints it is the largest GE here and rates for up to 5,000 square feet, double the 2,500 or so square feet you would ask of the 25-pint. For a below-grade basement with a moderate problem it is the safe choice. The tank is still available if you prefer to empty by hand.

Ownership centers on the pump hose and filter. Keep the hose free of kinks, wash the filter regularly and test the pump when the humid season starts. The plain 50-pint GE below skips the pump at a lower cost. A practical detail on pump models is where the discharge hose ends. Run it to a laundry standpipe, a utility sink or an outdoor port with a slight downward finish, and secure it so the end cannot lift out and spray the floor.
products.bestFor: Below-grade basements without a floor drain nearby.
pros: Pump lifts water up to 15 feet vertically
Smart Dry fan quiets down as humidity falls
Rated for spaces up to 5,000 square feet
Tank option remains if you prefer it
cons: Pump is an extra part that can fail

products.name: GE 50-Pint Dehumidifier for Basements, 5,000 Sq Ft
products.description:
The plain 50-pint shares the pumped model's coil, capacity and 5,000 square foot rating but leaves out the pump. That makes it the better choice when the basement has a floor drain at or below the machine's level, because a gravity hose does the same job with one fewer part.

Smart Dry fan control and a humidistat are standard, and the tank gives a fallback if you do not want a hose. Compared with the 35-pint GE, it carries 15 more pints of rated capacity, which is the margin that matters in a damp space.

The tradeoff is flexibility. If the drain is uphill, you are limited to the tank, which fills quickly at 50 pints in a wet room. If you do have a drain, this is the most economical way into a large-room GE. One caution applies to every 50-pint machine in a basement: the cabinet is wide and the intake sits low, so position it with several inches of clearance and keep stored boxes away from the grille. A blocked intake looks like a weak machine when it is really a placement problem, and moving it a foot from the wall often changes the readings.
products.bestFor: Basements with a floor drain that need 50-pint capacity.
pros: 50-pint capacity at a lower cost than the pumped model
Smart Dry fan reduces noise
Gravity hose or tank drain options
Humidistat holds a target
cons: No pump, so drain must be downhill
Tank fills quickly in a wet room

products.name: GE 50-Pint Wi-Fi Smart Dehumidifier, Alexa and Google
products.description:
The Wi-Fi 50-pint adds app and voice assistant control to the same capacity class. A full-bucket alert tells you when the tank needs emptying, an auto-shutoff switch protects the floor and automatic restart returns the unit to its previous setting after a power cut.

Automatic defrost is a practical point for basements that run cool: the machine clears coil frost and keeps pulling water instead of stalling. Smart Dry adjusts the fan the way the other 50-pint GEs do.

There is no pump here, so the app is the upgrade, not the drain. For a basement you rarely visit, the bucket alert alone justifies it. If the drain is uphill, step up to the pumped model instead. When you set up the app, confirm you can still read and change the target at the unit's own panel. A smart appliance that depends on a home network for every adjustment is more fragile than one that treats the app as an optional layer. Pair it with a separate hygrometer in the farthest corner so you can compare what the app reports against a second reading.
products.bestFor: Large basements checked from a phone rather than in person.
pros: Wi-Fi with Alexa and Google voice control
Full bucket alert prevents surprises
Auto restart resumes the saved setting
Automatic defrost helps in cool rooms
cons: Smart features raise the cost over the plain 50-pint

products.name: GE 35-Pint Dehumidifier with Drain Hose, 3,000 Sq Ft
products.description:
The 35-pint GE is the middle step: more capacity than the 25-pint and less bulk than the 50-pint. Coverage is listed at up to 3,000 square feet, and a built-in drain hose connection makes continuous drain easy to set up.

Smart Dry cuts fan speed as the room dries, which keeps noise manageable in a bedroom or finished room. In practice this model suits a medium basement or a large bedroom where the problem is steady but not severe.

It is also the one to choose when you want to move the machine often. The cabinet is smaller than the 50-pint models, and the tank is lighter to carry. For a damp, unfinished basement, step up a size. The tank on a mid-size unit is the thing you will notice most in ownership. In a room that sits near 65 percent humidity it can fill in well under a day, so decide early whether you will run the hose or commit to emptying daily. Most owners who start with the tank end up on the hose within a month, because a full tank shuts the unit off and the room drifts back up.
products.bestFor: Medium basements and large bedrooms with a steady humidity problem.
pros: 35-pint capacity balances size and output
Built-in drain hose connection for continuous use
Smart Dry fan lowers noise
Lighter and easier to move than the 50-pint
cons: Not enough for a wet unfinished basement
Smaller tank fills sooner than the 50-pint

products.name: GE 25-Pint Small Dehumidifier, 1,500 Sq Ft
products.description:
The 25-pint is the entry GE, rated for up to 1,500 square feet and built for bedrooms, bathrooms and small basements. It keeps the Smart Dry fan and a built-in drain hose connection, which is more than many small units offer.

Against the 35-pint, it gives up 10 pints and about 1,500 square feet of listed coverage. That is fine in a single room but undersized in an open basement.

It is the easiest to live with: lighter, quieter and simpler to store. Use the hose port if you cannot empty the tank daily, and clean the filter monthly. If you are choosing between this and the 35-pint for a bedroom, check the bedroom's door habits. A room that stays closed holds humidity well and the 25-pint will keep up, while a room with an open door to a damp hallway behaves like a bigger space and wants the 35-pint. Sizing for the air you actually share, not just the floor plan, avoids a unit that runs constantly.
pros: Lowest cost entry to the GE range
Built-in drain hose connection
Smart Dry fan keeps noise down
Light and easy to carry
cons: Too small for an open basement
Tank fills quickly in a damp space

buyingCriteria.explanation: GE sells 25, 35 and 50 pint steps, rated for roughly 1,500, 3,000 and 5,000 square feet. A bedroom or bathroom suits the 25-pint, a medium room the 35-pint and a basement the 50-pint. If the room smells musty, go one step up. A common mistake is reading the coverage figure as a promise: the 5,000 square foot label on the 50-pint assumes open floor and a mild problem, so a basement chopped into rooms by closed doors behaves like several small spaces and may need a second machine.

The pumped 50-pint lifts water 15 feet vertically, while the plain 50-pint and 35-pint rely on gravity. The pump matters only if the drain is uphill. If a floor drain is within reach, the cheaper model works the same. Before ordering, measure the vertical distance from the machine's drain port to the discharge point, because a run that climbs more than 15 feet exceeds what the pump on the top model can lift, and a long horizontal run also reduces the effective lift.

Smart Dry changes fan speed to match humidity, which reduces noise once the room is under control. It appears across the whole lineup. In a finished room that quiet cycle is worth more than a raw pint number. The fan still runs at full speed while the room is far above the target, so expect the loudest period right after a rainy spell or after hanging laundry nearby, and place the machine away from where you sleep or work.

The Wi-Fi 50-pint adds app and voice control plus a full-bucket alert. It helps for rentals and basements you rarely check. The local humidistat should still work if the network drops. For a second home or rental, the full bucket alert on the Wi-Fi 50-pint is the single feature that prevents a shut-off unit from sitting idle for a week while mold gets a start.

Compressor units lose output as the coil frosts in cool spaces. The Wi-Fi 50-pint lists automatic defrost, and a basement at 60F benefits. Without defrost, a unit can sit running with little output. If your basement sits below 60F for much of the year, consider a heated space strategy or a different technology, since no compressor model recovers well when the coil is constantly near freezing.

The 25 and 35 pint models include a built-in hose connection, while the 50-pint models offer tank or continuous drain. A tank at 50 pints can fill in under a day in a wet room. Set up a hose if you can. Even a short hose into a bucket-sized floor drain turns a daily chore into a once-a-season check.

howWeEvaluated.title: Capacity ladder
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared the 25, 35 and 50 pint steps and their listed coverage of 1,500, 3,000 and 5,000 square feet. A clear ladder makes sizing easier. We treated ratings as spec sheet figures.

howWeEvaluated.title: Drain options
howWeEvaluated.description: We looked at the pump on the top model and the hose connection on the smaller units. For rooms with awkward drain layouts, the pump model scored highest. Gravity hoses scored well for simplicity.

howWeEvaluated.title: Smart features
howWeEvaluated.description: We assessed Wi-Fi, voice control and alerts on the smart 50-pint. These help for remote spaces. A working local humidistat is the baseline.

howWeEvaluated.title: Cool-room performance
howWeEvaluated.description: We noted automatic defrost on the Wi-Fi model and considered how cool basements affect output. Defrost keeps the machine productive at lower temperatures.

howWeEvaluated.title: Value across the range
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared relative price tiers from the 35-pint at the lower end through the pumped 50-pint at the top. Value goes to the smallest GE that still handles the room.

cards.label: Pump (GE 50-Pint with Pump)
cards.text: Lifts water 15 feet and solves uphill drains. It adds a part and a cost. It suits below-grade basements.

cards.label: Gravity hose (GE 25, 35, 50 Pint)
cards.text: Simpler and cheaper with no extra part to fail. It needs a downhill path to the drain. The 25 and 35 pint models include a hose connection.

howToChoose.note: Choose the pump only when the drain is uphill.

cards.label: Look for
cards.text: At least 50 pints for a moderately damp basement, a drain that works with gravity or a pump and defrost for cool rooms. Place it with room around the intake.

cards.label: In this comparison
cards.text: The 50-Pint with Pump is the all-rounder, the plain 50-Pint is the value choice with a floor drain and the Wi-Fi 50-Pint suits remote monitoring.

cards.label: Spend more if
cards.text: The drain is uphill or you want remote status. The pumped and Wi-Fi 50-pint models earn their cost.

cards.label: Save if
cards.text: The room is small or has a floor drain. The 25-Pint, 35-Pint or plain 50-Pint do the job.

maintenance.why: A clogged filter restricts airflow and invites coil frost. Rinse and dry it fully.
Standing water grows slime and odor. Use mild soap.
Kinks and a stuck pump cause overflow. Run a test cycle.
Dust cuts heat transfer. Unplug the unit first.
A separate hygrometer confirms the unit's built-in reading.

faq.q: Which GE size do I need?
faq.a: A bedroom or bathroom suits the 25-pint, a medium basement the 35-pint and a large basement the 50-pint. If the room is chronically damp, go one step up.

faq.q: Is the pump model worth it?
faq.a: Only if your drain is uphill or on another level. With a floor drain nearby, the plain 50-pint does the same work for less.
No. It adds remote control and alerts, not capacity. It is useful for spaces you do not visit often.

faq.q: Do GE dehumidifiers work in cool basements?
faq.a: They work best above about 65F. The Wi-Fi 50-pint lists auto defrost, which helps when the coil would otherwise frost.

Compressor units commonly run 5 to 10 years. Cleaning the filter and coil is the main lever, and an undersized unit wears faster. Setting the machine on a small riser keeps it off damp concrete, and keeping the cabinet level helps the bucket float switch read correctly. Replace any hose that has gone stiff or cloudy, since a cracked line is the most common leak.

Between 40 and 50 percent is typical. Many owners aim for 45 percent in summer and let it drift to the low 40s in winter. Above 60 percent encourages mold and below 30 percent feels dry. Set the unit near the upper middle of that range, since a setpoint at the extreme low end makes the compressor run almost nonstop.
